steps.title: A nested loop, no index
steps.caption: No index on order_events.order_id: the nested loop rescans all 1,500,000 events for every order.
steps.body: Customer 2 has 45 orders since 1 September, and the query fetches each one's latest event with a `LATERAL` subquery, which runs once per order: a **nested loop**. `order_events` has no index on `order_id` (a foreign key doesn't create one), so each of the 45 loops is a full scan of 1,500,000 events: 67.5 million rows and 496,350 page reads for 45 result rows, 1.8 s in one run on a laptop.

steps.title: Nested loop + index
steps.caption: Joined to order_items, each of the 45 orders is one index lookup: root, branch, leaf, heap page.
steps.body: The same 45 orders joined to their items: the inner side is an index scan on `order_items_pkey`, so each outer row costs one descent of the three-level B-tree plus a heap page, 182 pages for 45 lookups and 117 rows in 14 ms (most of it the scan of `orders`). A nested loop wins when the outer side is small and the inner join column is indexed: about N × log M work, and the first row comes back at once.

steps.title: Hash join, merge join
steps.caption: Hash: build on September's orders, probe with every item. Merge: walk two sorted inputs together.
steps.body: **Hash join** (revenue per category in September): PostgreSQL builds a hash table on the smaller input, 23,436 orders in 32,768 buckets (1,216 kB, one batch), then reads all 1,250,000 order items once and probes it: 58,590 match, 84 ms. With `work_mem` cut to 64 kB it splits into 8 batches that spill to disk, 293 ms. **Merge join** (orders 100,001–300,000): both inputs come out of their primary key indexes in `order_id` order, so one pass over each joins them: 500,000 rows, no sort, 262 ms.

steps.title: How the planner picks
steps.caption: The planner costs every method from its row estimates and keeps the cheapest one for each join.
steps.body: For each join order and method the planner estimates a cost from its row estimates and keeps the cheapest; the bars are its estimates for each query with the other methods switched off. A wrong row estimate can pick the wrong method, past 8 tables (`join_collapse_limit`) it partly keeps the JOIN order you wrote, and from 12 (`geqo_threshold`) it searches with a genetic algorithm. MySQL 8.4 has nested loops and, since 8.0.18, hash joins, but no merge join.
